opener.dateline: [From the South Pacific Times, Thursday, September 5, 1878.]

div.p: It is satisfactory to us to remark, in our present review, that perfect harmony apparently exists among the high powers of the state, a circumstance which, in spite of the several antagonistical demonstrations recently made by the one side and the other, guarantees that peace will be maintained at all hazards.

We have frequently stated the fact that we make it a rule to eschew political matters; but as the most notable event of the week has been the arrival of Don Manuel Pardo, the ex-president of the republic and chief of the Civil party, after a prolonged absence in Chili, and all the journals make it their chief topic of remark, we must necessarily allude at some length to so important a circumstance, in order to give a comprehensive idea of the effect likely to be produced thereby on the present political situation.

Señor Pardo is the center of that party now dominant in the Chamber of Representatives, which has so recently given evidence of its strength in the elections, and in the adherence to its principles of the chief capitalists and representatives of the higher classes of society in the republic.

Mr. Pardo was elected, during his absence, president of the Senate, and he has, in all probability, returned to occupy himself with the duties of his important office, and at the same time to strengthen and unify his party, and prevent any possibility of dissension among the numerous partisans of what is known here as “Civilismo.”

It will be remembered that fourteen months ago Señor Pardo voluntarily left the country, in order to avoid serious complications, which it was thought his presence here would give rise to, and which at one time caused the government also to be apprehensive.

Since then, however, it may be remarked that Mr. Pardo has abstained from any interference with the course of political affairs here, holding himself entirely aloof;
but his partisans having invested him with the representation in Congress of one of the departments of the republic, his patriotic feelings have compelled him to return, in order to fulfill his duties. Hence he has abandoned his self-imposed exile, and is once more among his friends. His arrival here on the 2d instant was marked by an enthusiastic ovation in his honor; and, although some little show of opposition was made by a few of his political opponents, the powerful support of his friends on the one hand, and the effective precaution taken by the local police authorities on the other, prevented any obstacle being opposed to his peaceable return to his home. Since his arrival he has received the congratulations of his excellency the President, an act of courtesy to which he responded by going in person to call upon General Prado on the day of his arrival. The interview which took place lasted about half an hour, but as it was entirely private nothing is publicly known as to its purport. Many comments, however, have been made by the press as to the existence of a future good understanding.
